passages.title: The Overwhelming Day and the faces of the damned
passages.tafsir:
## The Day that covers everything

This passage opens Sūrat al-Ghāshiyah with a question addressed to the Prophet ﷺ — "Has the news of the Overwhelming Event reached you?" — and then answers it with a portrait of one group of people on that Day: faces downcast and humiliated, worn out by labour that earned them nothing, entering a scorching Fire where the only drink is boiling water and the only food a thorny plant that neither nourishes nor stills hunger. What binds ayat 1–7 together is a single, sobering idea: on the Day that overwhelms all people, there will be those whose whole life's effort turns out to have been spent for nothing.

## Al-Ghāshiyah: why the Day is called "the Overwhelming"

Ibn Kathir records from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd that *al-Ghāshiyah* is one of the names of the Day of Judgement. It has been called this, he explains, "because it will overwhelm the people and overcome them." Nothing and no one stands outside it.

The passage begins as a question — "Has the news of the Overwhelming Event reached you?" — drawing the listener in before the scene unfolds. And the Prophet's ﷺ own practice shows how central this surah was to public worship: it is reported on the authority of An-Nu'man bin Bashir that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite Sūrat al-A'lā (87) and al-Ghāshiyah in the 'Id and Friday prayers; Imam Malik recorded that when Ad-Dahhak bin Qays asked An-Nu'man bin Bashir what the Prophet ﷺ recited on Friday alongside Sūrat al-Jumu'ah, he replied, "Al-Ghashiyah." This narration is recorded by Abu Dawud, An-Nasa'i, Muslim and Ibn Majah. Week after week, festival after festival, the community was made to hear this warning afresh.

## Faces that tell the whole story (ayat 2–3)

The Qur'an does not begin with the Fire; it begins with faces. In ayah 2, *khāshi'ah* — "downcast" — comes from the root *khushā'*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains as meaning to humble, humiliate, cast down; it is the same word used for casting oneself down before Allah in prayer. There is a piercing irony in the choice: people who would not lower themselves before Allah in this world will find their faces lowered on that Day — but now in humiliation and disgrace, not devotion. Qatadah glossed the word simply as "humiliated," and Ibn 'Abbas added the crucial point: "They will be humble, but this action will be of no benefit to them." Humility offered too late earns nothing.

Ayah 3 gives two more descriptions: *'āmilah nāṣibah*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up both words. *'Āmilah* describes a person who works continuously until completely tired; *nāṣibah*, from *naṣab*, describes one who toils unceasingly to the point of total exhaustion. These are not idle people. They are people who worked themselves to the bone.

**Where did all that labour happen?** The commentators offer two readings, and both are worth holding together:

- 'Ikrimah and As-Suddi said it means "laboring in the worldly life with disobedience, and weariness in the Fire from torment and perdition" — a life of sinful striving followed by an eternity of exhausting punishment.
- Qurtubi and other commentators, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, held that the downcast faces belong to the Hereafter while the working and exhaustion belong to this world — for the Hereafter is not a realm where one labours to the point of weariness. On this reading, the ayah describes people who genuinely exerted themselves in devotion — enduring real hardship, sincerely seeking Allah's pleasure — but on wrong and idolatrous paths, like the monks and ascetics Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions as examples. Their effort was real; its foundation was false; so it was not accepted. Al-Bukhari records that Ibn 'Abbas said of this ayah simply: "The Christians."

## 'Umar's tears at the monastery

Nothing conveys the weight of these two ayat like the reaction of 'Umar bin al-Khattab. Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Burqani narrated from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni that 'Umar passed by the monastery of a monk and called out to him. When the monk came out, 'Umar looked at him and began to weep. Asked why, the Commander of the Faithful replied that he had remembered the statement of Allah: "Laboring, weary. They will enter into Fire, Hamiyah" — "So that is what has made me cry."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates a similar account from Hasan al-Basri about 'Umar in Syria: an old monk came to him, his face exhausted from religious exercises, his body dry, his clothing miserable. 'Umar wept and said, "I pity the condition of this old man. This poor soul worked so hard and showed such readiness to lay down his life to achieve a particular purpose — but, alas! He could not achieve it," and then he recited these very verses. 'Umar's tears are the right response to this passage: not contempt for the misguided, but grief at sincere effort poured into a vessel that cannot hold it.

## The Fire, the drink, the food (ayat 4–7)

The passage now follows those weary faces into their destination, and the scene unfolds as one continuous deprivation: a Fire without relief, a drink that scalds, a food that fails. The Fire is called *ḥāmiyah*, which Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah explain as "hot with intense heat." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks the obvious question: heat is the natural property of fire, so why mention it? The answer: to signal that the fire of Hell cannot be compared to the fire of this world. Worldly fire eventually dims or dies out; the Fire of Hell is everlasting — its heat will neither reduce nor end.

Within that Fire, even drink becomes torment. The spring they are given to drink from is *āniyah* — water whose heat "has reached its maximum limit and boiling point," as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and As-Suddi explained.

And their only food is from *ḍarī'*. Ibn 'Abbas (in the report of Ali bin Abi Talhah) called it "a tree from the Hellfire." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Jawza' and Qatadah identified it with *ash-shibriq*, a plant the Arabs knew well: Qatadah said the Quraysh called it *ash-shabraq* in spring and *aḍ-ḍarī'* in summer; 'Ikrimah described it as a thorny tree reaching down to the ground; and al-Bukhari relates from Mujahid that the people of the Hijaz call it *ḍarī'* when it dries, and it is poisonous. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that in this world no animal will even go near it — foul-smelling, poisonous, and thorny. Sa'id narrated from Qatadah that he said of it: "This is of the worst, most disgusting and loathsome of foods." The Qur'an named a plant its first hearers could picture — the ugliest forage of their own landscape — to give them a taste of the Hereafter in the vocabulary of their world.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises two questions here. First: how can a plant survive in fire? The answer given is that the Creator who sustained plants in this world with water and air has the power to make the fire itself their nutrient. Second: elsewhere the Qur'an names *zaqqūm* and *ghislīn* as the food of Hell — how can this ayah say there is "no food except ḍarī'"? The answer is that the restriction contrasts with palatable food: the people of the Fire will have nothing fit for consumption, only the worst and most loathsome kinds, of which ḍarī' is an example that includes the others. Qurtubi also suggested that Hell may have different levels, with different food on each level.

The final ayah of the passage answers the mockers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that when the preceding ayah was revealed, some of the pagans of Makkah mockingly said that their camels eat ḍarī' and remain fat and healthy. The next ayah came down in response: do not compare the ḍarī' of this world with that of the Hereafter — it "will neither nourish nor satisfy hunger." Ibn Kathir puts it precisely: the very purpose of eating will not be achieved, and no harm will be repelled by it. Hunger will remain; only the torment of eating is added to it.

## Living it

The passage's warning is exact, and 'Umar understood it: effort alone saves no one. A person can labour, sacrifice, and exhaust themselves in devotion — and arrive on the Overwhelming Day with a downcast face, because the labour was not built on truth. The faces in ayah 2 belong to those "who did not cast themselves down before Allah in this world," as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it — so the practical demand of these ayat is to practise *khushū'* now, willingly, in prayer and submission, so that it is not extracted later in humiliation. And the Prophet's ﷺ habit of reciting this surah every Friday suggests how often we need the reminder: not once in a lifetime, but week after week.

passages.title: The radiant faces and the delights of Paradise
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the sūrah's turn from sorrow to joy. Ibn Kathir marks the transition explicitly: "After mentioning the situation of the wretched people, Allah changes the discussion to mention those who will be happy." From here to the end of the passage, Allah shows us the faces of the people of Paradise — radiant with bliss — and then walks us, almost room by room, through the Garden prepared for them: its height, its peace, its springs, its couches, cups, cushions and carpets. What holds ayat 8–16 together is a single sustained portrait: first the *people* of Paradise (ayat 8–9), then their *place* (ayat 10–11), then its *furnishings* (ayat 12–16).

## Ayah 8: faces glowing with bliss

"On that Day other faces will be glowing with bliss" (*wujūhun yawmaʾidhin nāʿimah*). Ibn Kathir explains that "pleasure will be noticeable in them": the bliss of these people is so complete that it shows on their faces. Their delight cannot be hidden — it is written on their features for all to see.

## Ayah 9: joy earned, not stumbled into

Why are these faces radiant? Ayah 9 answers: they are "fully pleased with their striving" (*li-saʿyihā rāḍiyah*). Ibn Kathir stresses that their joy "will only occur due to their striving," and cites Sufyan: "They will be pleased with their deeds." This is a quietly weighty point. In the world, effort for Allah's sake can feel costly and its results uncertain; on that Day, the believer will look back at every act of endeavour and feel nothing but satisfaction. The deeds that once required struggle become the very source of delight — no regret, no wishing they had done otherwise, only contentment with what they sent ahead.

## Ayat 10–11: a high place, and a healed atmosphere

Ayah 10 places them "in a lofty Paradise" (*jannah ʿāliyah*). Ibn Kathir explains this as "elevated and brilliant, secure in their dwellings" — height here carries the sense of honour, splendour and safety all at once.

Then comes ayah 11, and it is striking what the Qur'an chooses to mention first about this exalted Garden — not gold or rivers, but silence from ugliness: "where no idle talk will be heard" (*lā tasmaʿu fīhā lāghiyah*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks what this futile, harmful speech includes: "the words of disbelief, futile or idle talk, obscene language, calumny or false accusation, or any other talk that hurts people's feelings." Ibn Kathir shows this is a recurring promise of the Qur'an, pairing our ayah with "They shall not hear therein any Laghw, but only Salam" (19:62), "Free from any Laghw, and free from sin" (52:23), and "No Laghw will they hear therein, nor any sinful speech. But only the saying of: 'Salam! Salam!'" (56:25–26).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson out beautifully: the fact that Allah counts this among the *blessings* of Paradise "shows that false accusation and absurd talks are hurtful." Freedom from wounding, foolish words is presented as a delight on par with springs and couches — because such words, as the commentary says, are the kind that "may pollute their hearts." Anyone who has been worn down by mockery, slander or endless empty chatter knows that a place where the ears are entirely at rest is itself a profound mercy.

## Ayah 12: springs, not a spring

"In it will be a running spring" (*fīhā ʿaynun jāriyah*). The word is singular, but Ibn Kathir explains that the singular here is used "with the intent of emphasizing affirmation. It is not intended to mean that there is only one spring... the meaning is that in it (Paradise) are flowing springs" — water flowing freely, everywhere.

On the waters of Paradise, Ibn Kathir cites a hadith recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The rivers of Paradise spring forth from beneath hills — or mountains — of musk." Even the source of Paradise's water is fragrance.

## Ayat 13–16: the furnishings of honour

The passage then surveys the interior of this Garden, and each item carries a descriptive word worth pausing on.

**Thrones raised high (ayah 13).** Ibn Kathir describes these *surur marfūʿah* as "lofty, delightful, numerous couches, with elevated ceilings," upon which the wide-eyed, beautiful maidens of Paradise will be seated. He also relates a touching detail that has been mentioned: whenever the friend of Allah wishes to sit on these lofty thrones, "they (the thrones) will lower themselves for him." Even the furniture of Paradise serves its people — elevation without any strain to reach it.

**Cups set at hand (ayah 14).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the vocabulary: *akwāb* is the plural of *kūb*, a goblet, glass or cup for drinking water, and *mawḍūʿah* means "well placed" — set in their due places, close to the water. Ibn Kathir adds that these vessels are "prepared and presented for whoever among their masters (i.e., the people of Paradise) wants them." No one thirsts and then searches; the cup is already there.

**Cushions lined up (ayah 15).** For *namāriq*, Ibn Kathir transmits the explanation of Ibn 'Abbas: "An-Namariq are pillows" — an interpretation shared by 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, As-Suddi, Ath-Thawri and others. And they are *maṣfūfah*, arranged in rows: order and abundance together.

**Carpets spread out (ayah 16).** For *zarābiyy*, Ibn 'Abbas again explains: "Az-Zarabi are carpets," as Ad-Dahhak and others also said. The word *mabthūthah* ("spread out"), Ibn Kathir notes, means they are "placed here and there for whoever would like to sit upon them." Wherever a person of Paradise wishes to rest, comfort is already waiting.

Notice the progression: rest (thrones), refreshment (cups), recline (cushions), and a floor of luxury underfoot (carpets). Nothing must be asked for; everything has been anticipated.

## Living it: the "etiquette of living" hidden in a single word

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a remarkably practical lesson from ayah 14 under the heading "Etiquette of Living." The cups of Paradise are praised for being *mawḍūʿah* — well placed, near the water. From this the commentary derives an adab (a rule of refined conduct) for our own homes: drinking vessels ought to be kept in their designated place near the water, not misplaced so that household members must hunt for them when they wish to drink — "this situation is irritating." The same applies to other items of daily use — cans, glasses, towels — which should be arranged in their proper places and returned there after use, so that no one in the household faces difficulty finding them. All of this, the commentary says, "is deducible from the word maudu'ah 'well placed', because Allah has arranged the goblets near the water for the comfort of the inmates of Paradise."

It is a lovely instance of how the Qur'an teaches: even a description of the Hereafter models a courtesy for this world. Allah honours His servants in Paradise by sparing them the smallest inconvenience — and a believer imitates that generosity, in miniature, by keeping a home in which others are spared inconvenience too.

## Reading the passage whole

Taken together, ayat 8–16 are the answer to the wretchedness Ibn Kathir says was mentioned before: Allah turns the discussion "to mention those who will be happy," and the portrait He paints is complete. Faces glow from striving they are pleased with; their Garden is high and secure; nothing ugly reaches their ears; springs flow freely; and thrones, cups, cushions and carpets stand ready before anyone asks. The passage invites the believer to strive now, in full confidence that on that Day the striving itself will be a source of joy — and that everything after it has already been prepared.

passages.title: Signs of Allah's design in camels, sky, mountains, earth
passages.tafsir:
## Four signs in plain sight

After describing the Hereafter, Sūrat al-Ghāshiyah turns the listener's eyes to the visible present. In ayat 17–20 Allah poses four questions built on a single pattern: do they not look — at the camels, how they were created; at the sky, how it was raised high; at the mountains, how they were firmly set up; at the earth, how it was levelled out? These are not four random wonders. As the commentaries explain, they form one connected summons: the everyday world of the listener, examined honestly, testifies to the power and greatness of its Maker.

## Why this argument, and why here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the placement. The sūrah first described the conditions of the Hereafter, the reward of the believers and the retribution of the unbelievers. Now it turns to rebuff the obdurate unbelievers' denial of the Hereafter — they rejected it on the ground that after death and the decomposition of the body and bones, it is inconceivable that they could be recomposed and resurrected. For their guidance, Allah invites their attention to reflect carefully on a few of His Signs. The universe holds uncountable such signs; these verses single out four **which suited the condition of the desert Arabs**. They often travelled through the desert, and in that situation all they saw were the camels they travelled on; above them was the sky, beneath them the earth, and all around them — left, right, front and back — the mountains. The Arabs are commanded to ponder over these four natural phenomena which make Allah's might manifest. Ibn Kathir makes the same point: Allah "directs the bedouin to consider what he himself witnesses" — his camel that he rides upon, the sky that is above his head, the mountain that faces him, and the earth that is under him.

## Ayah 17 — the camels

Ibn Kathir notes that the Arabs are reminded of the camel because it was their most common domestic animal, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that although the elephant is a much larger animal, Allah mentioned the camel rather than the elephant because the Arabs knew camels and scarcely saw an elephant.

Ibn Kathir calls the camel "an amazing creation", fashioned in a strange and wondrous way: extremely powerful and strong, yet gentle — it carries heavy loads yet allows itself to be guided by a weak rider; it is eaten, benefit is derived from its hair, and its milk is drunk. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the design in detail. Among animals it is the largest, most robust and durable, yet even a poor bedouin does not find it difficult to look after: let loose, it gathers its own nutriment and lives on leaves, its long neck reaching the tops of high trees, whereas the food of elephants and other animals works out expensive. In the Arabian deserts, where water is scarce, Allah's Power provided it with a small narrow-mouthed pouch in its paunch that stores up extra water, so it can survive for about a week without drinking. Allah has divided its legs into three levels, each leg with two knees that it manoeuvres to sit down, so riders climb up and down without any ladder. It is the chief beast of burden in the deserts, carrying large loads; and while the scorching sun makes daytime travel in Arabia most difficult, Allah has made it possible for the camel to keep travelling the whole night. Camels are so obedient that even a little child can lead them along anywhere. All of this, the commentary concludes, teaches man that Allah is Omnipotent and has consummate wisdom.

Ibn Kathir also records that Shurayh al-Qāḍī used to say, "Come out with us so that we may look at the camels and how they were created, and at the sky and how it has been raised."

## Ayat 18–20 — sky, mountains, earth

**The sky (ayah 18):** Ibn Kathir explains "how it is raised" as: how Allah raised it in such magnificence above the ground, and links it to Allah's words elsewhere: "Have they not looked at the heaven above them, how We have made it and adorned it and there are no rifts in it?" (50:6).

**The mountains (ayah 19):** "how they are rooted" means, Ibn Kathir says, how they have been erected — firmly affixed **so that the earth does not sway with its dwellers**. And Allah made them with the benefits and minerals they contain. Power and provision in the same object.

**The earth (ayah 20):** "how it is outspread" means how it has been spread out, extended and made smooth.

## Where the argument lands

Ibn Kathir states the conclusion the four signs are meant to force: all of this is proof of the power of the Creator and Maker of these things, and should lead the onlooker to see that He is the Lord, the Most Great, the Creator, the Owner and the Controller of everything — "therefore, He is the One other than Whom none deserves to be worshipped." The chain of reasoning runs from observation, to recognising the Maker's power, to tawḥīd — that is, worshipping Him alone.

## From the Sunnah: the bedouin who reasoned exactly this way

Ibn Kathir attaches to these ayat the story of Ḍimām bin Thaʿlabah, because the very things this passage points to — heaven, earth, mountains — are what Ḍimām swore by when he questioned the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Imam Ahmad recorded from Thābit, from Anas, that the Companions had been prohibited from asking the Messenger of Allah ﷺ anything, so it used to amaze them when an intelligent man of the desert would come and ask while they listened. A bedouin came and said: "O Muhammad! Verily, your messenger has come to us and he claims that you claim that Allah sent you." The Prophet ﷺ said, "He told the truth." The man asked: "Who created the heaven?" — "Allah." "Who created the earth?" — "Allah." "Who erected these mountains and placed in them whatever is in them?" — "Allah." Then he said: "By the One Who created the heaven, the earth, and erected these mountains — did Allah send you?" He ﷺ said, "Yes." The man then confirmed, oath by oath, the five daily prayers, the charity due on wealth, and the pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way there, and turned to leave saying: "By He Who has sent you with the truth, I will not add anything to these things and I will not decrease anything from them." The Prophet ﷺ said: "If he has spoken truthfully, he will certainly enter Paradise." This hadith was recorded by Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

A desert Arab moved from the created heaven, earth and mountains to certainty about the One who made them, and from that certainty to accepting the messenger and what he brought — the very reflection these ayat call for.

## Living it

The passage asks for something anyone can do today: deliberate, careful reflection on the ordinary world — the animal, the sky, the mountain, the ground underfoot — until observation ripens into recognition of the Creator's power and wisdom, and recognition into worshipping Him alone, for He is "the One other than Whom none deserves to be worshipped." Shurayh al-Qāḍī's words remain an open invitation: "Come out with us so that we may look at the camels and how they were created, and at the sky and how it has been raised."

passages.title: The Prophet reminds; Allah alone judges and reckons
passages.tafsir:
# The Reminder and the Reckoning — Sūrat al-Ghāshiyah 88:21–26

These closing ayat of Sūrat al-Ghāshiyah define, in six short lines, the entire division of labour between the Prophet ﷺ and his Lord: the Prophet's task is to remind, and nothing more; calling people to account and requiting them belongs to Allah alone. What holds the passage together is a single boundary drawn twice — first around the Prophet's mission (ayat 21–22: remind, but do not compel), then around Allah's exclusive right (ayat 25–26: to Us is their return, with Us is their reckoning).

## "So remind — you are only one who reminds" (ayat 21–22)

The sūrah has just directed its listeners to look at four things any desert Arab could see without moving: the camel he rides, the sky above him, the mountains before him, the earth beneath him (ayat 17–20). Ibn Kathir says Allah directs the bedouin to consider what he himself witnesses — his camel, the sky above his head, the mountain that faces him, the earth under him — all of it proof of the power of the Creator and Maker of these things, things that should lead him to see that He is the Lord, the Most Great, the Creator, the Owner, and the Controller of everything, and therefore the One other than Whom none deserves to be worshipped.

Then, in a separate section he titles "The Messenger ﷺ is only Charged with Delivering the Message," Ibn Kathir explains ayah 21: "O Muhammad! Remind the people with what you have been sent with to them." The ayah names the Prophet ﷺ a *mudhakkir* — one who reminds — and the sentence is deliberately restrictive: "you are **only** one who reminds." Ayah 22 then makes the same point explicit from the other side: *lasta ʿalayhim bi-muṣayṭir*, "You are not a *muṣayṭir* over them."

What is a *muṣayṭir*? The early authorities cited by Ibn Kathir gloss it vividly. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and others said: "You are not a dictator over them" — meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains, you cannot create faith in their hearts. Ibn Zayd said: "You are not the one who can force them to have faith." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "taskmaster": "You are not a taskmaster set up over them." However the word is turned, the sense is one: the Prophet ﷺ cannot compel belief into existence in anyone's heart.

Ibn Kathir ties this directly to a parallel ayah: "your duty is only to convey (the Message) and on Us is the reckoning" (13:40). Conveying is the Prophet's charge; the reckoning is Allah's. That same pairing is exactly what ayat 21–22 and 25–26 of this sūrah spell out.

## A comfort, not merely a limit

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 22 as consolation. The sūrah ends, it says, with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ being *comforted*: he is told that he is only a preacher, and as such he must keep on preaching — and he should not worry beyond that. It is for Allah to call the unbelievers to Him to render account of their deeds and actions, and to punish them accordingly.

## The Prophet ﷺ himself recited these ayat — the hadith of Jabir

Ibn Kathir records how the Prophet ﷺ applied this very passage. Imam Ahmad recorded from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say *Lā ilāha illallāh* (none has the right to be worshipped except Allah). So if they say that, they have safeguarded their blood and wealth from me — except for what is rightfully due from it — and their reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." Then he ﷺ recited: "So remind them — you are only one who reminds. You are not a *muṣayṭir* over them." Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim recorded this hadith in his Book of Faith, that At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i recorded it in the Books of Tafsir in their Sunans, and that it can be found in both of the Sahihs.

Notice what the Prophet's ﷺ own recitation joins together: once a person says the testimony of faith, his blood and wealth are safeguarded — "except for what is rightfully due from it" — and "their reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." What lies inside the heart is left to Allah, exactly as ayah 22 declares: the Prophet ﷺ is not a *muṣayṭir* who can reach into hearts, and the accounting for hearts was never his to perform.

## The reminder at work: Dimam bin Thaʿlabah

Ibn Kathir also connects this passage to a scene from the Prophet's ﷺ life. The things sworn by in the story, he notes, are the very signs of ayat 17–20: "These are the things Dimam swore by after questioning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Imam Ahmad recorded from Thabit, who reported that Anas said that the Companions had been prohibited from asking the Messenger of Allah ﷺ anything, so it delighted them when an intelligent man of the desert would come and ask while they listened. A bedouin came and said: your messenger claims that you claim that Allah sent you. "He told the truth." Who created the heaven? "Allah." Who created the earth? "Allah." Who erected these mountains and placed in them whatever is in them? "Allah." Then the man swore: "By the One Who created the heaven, the earth, and erected these mountains, did Allah send you?" — "Yes."

He then went through the obligations. Your messenger claims we must pray five prayers in our day and night. "He told the truth." — "By He Who has sent you, did Allah command you with this?" — "Yes." Your messenger claims we must give charity from our wealth. "He told the truth." — "By He Who has sent you, did Allah command you with this?" — "Yes." Your messenger claims we must perform pilgrimage (Hajj) to the House, for whoever is able to find a way there. "He told the truth." Then the man turned away to leave, saying: "By He Who has sent you with the truth, I will not add anything to these things and I will not decrease anything from them." The Prophet ﷺ said: "If he has spoken truthfully, he will certainly enter Paradise." Ibn Kathir notes this hadith was recorded by Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

The whole passage lives inside this story. Dimam swore by the signs of ayat 17–20 — heaven, earth, mountains. The Prophet ﷺ answered his questions truthfully and left him free; no compulsion appears anywhere in the exchange. And even when the man declared his commitment, the Prophet ﷺ said *if he has spoken truthfully* — leaving the man's inner sincerity, and his reward, with Allah.

## "But whoever turns away and disbelieves" (ayat 23–24)

The freedom not to be compelled is not freedom from consequence. Ayah 23 turns to "the one who turns away and disbelieves" — and Ibn Kathir unpacks the two verbs as covering both limbs and heart: he *turns away* from acting upon its pillars, and he *disbelieves* in the truth with his heart and his tongue. Ibn Kathir points to the parallel in the Qur'an: "So he neither believed nor prayed! But on the contrary, he belied and turned away!" (75:31–32) — rejection inside, abandonment outside.

For such a person, ayah 24: "Then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment" — *al-ʿadhāb al-akbar*. Note who the subject is: *Allah* will punish him. The threat is real and severe, but it is not the Prophet's ﷺ to execute; the same boundary drawn in ayah 22 holds even here.

## "To Us is their return; with Us is their reckoning" (ayat 25–26)

The sūrah closes with two solemn declarations. "Verily, to Us will be their return" — Ibn Kathir: their place of return and their resort. However far a person turns away in this life, there is only one destination. "Then verily, for Us will be their reckoning" — Ibn Kathir: "We will reckon their deeds for them and requite them for those deeds. If they did good, they will receive good, and if they did evil, they will receive evil."

The wording places "Us" first in both ayat — *to Us* their return, *with Us* their reckoning — sealing the theme of the whole passage: the return is to none but Allah, and the accounting rests with none but Him. This is the exact counterpart of ayah 21's restriction. The Prophet ﷺ is *only* a reminder; Allah is the One Who reckons. Between those two truths the whole passage stands.

## Living it

For anyone who conveys this religion — a parent, a teacher, a friend giving counsel — these ayat set both the duty and its limit. Keep reminding: ayah 21 is a command, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that the Prophet ﷺ "must keep on preaching." But do not appoint yourself a *muṣayṭir*: you cannot create faith in anyone's heart, and you were never asked to. Deliver the truth as the Prophet ﷺ did with Dimam — plainly, patiently, without coercion — and then release the outcome. Whoever accepts, and whoever turns away, both are travelling to the same Lord, "and their reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."
